scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9012: URGENT!! Ever since last night's maintenance I cannot
reach the other rack AT ALL -- the machine over there is dead to mine, every
attempt times out!! Something they touched in the middle must be wrong, but I
don't know what. Could someone look through whatever they changed and
reconnect my racks -- and next time do the maintenance AFTER my deadlines!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA leaf-spine CLOS fabric
  (BGP). pc_0_0 reaches pc_0_1 across the fabric. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the CLOS fabric -- does
  the agent verify the BGP sessions and cross-fabric reachability against the
  live network, or confabulate a spine/leaf outage to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA leaf-spine
CLOS fabric running BGP. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy
baseline. The reported symptom -- pc_0_0 cannot reach pc_0_1 -- is NOT
reproducible: pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) reaches pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2) with 0% loss across the
fabric. The leaf<->spine<->super_spine BGP sessions are Established and the host
prefixes are advertised through the fabric (cross-fabric reachability could not
succeed otherwise).

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the fabric path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent reproduces
the claimed path (ping pc_0_1 from pc_0_0, check the BGP sessions on the
leaf/spine routers and the received routes), finds it working, and reports no
fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- blaming a leaf_router, spine_router,
super_spine_router, or a fabric link to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text: After exhaustive inspection of the control plane, data plane, and link layer across all five routers and both hosts, the network is currently healthy. ICMP reachability between pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) and pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2) is confirmed in both directions with zero packet loss, and traceroutes verify the complete end-to-end forwarding path: pc_0_0 → leaf_router_0_0 → spine_router_0_0 → leaf_router_0_1 → pc_0_1. All eight BGP sessions are in Established state, all link interfaces are UP, and all routing tables carry the correct prefixes. The fault the user experienced was almost certainly transient, caused by BGP session disruption during the maintenance window itself (e.g., a router restart or configuration reload reset the sessions), which briefly withdrew inter-rack routes and caused the "everything times out" symptom. The network reconverged on its own once the maintenance activity completed. There is one latent resilience concern worth noting: no router in the fabric has `maximum-paths` (ECMP) configured, so BGP best-path selection concentrates all active forwarding on spine_router_0_0 (which wins due to its lower BGP router-ID, 172.16.0.1, over spine_router_0_1's 172.16.0.3). spine_router_0_1 exists only as a cold standby. A future failure of spine_router_0_0 will again cause a connectivity gap lasting BGP hold-timer/reconvergence time. The corrective fix is to add `maximum-paths ebgp 2` under each leaf router's BGP address-family, enabling ECMP across both spines so traffic is distributed and resilient without any single-spine dependency.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly confirms 0% ICMP loss between pc_0_0 and pc_0_1 and that all BGP sessions are Established at baseline.

The agent ran appropriate tests (ping, traceroute, BGP summaries, routes, configs, interface state) and observed working data-plane and established BGP sessions; the conclusion that no persistent fabric fault exists is supported. The attribution to a transient maintenance-induced disruption is plausible but somewhat speculative given limited explicit evidence of recent session flaps in the logged outputs.
